extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology and literary criticism; general readers interested in theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents the theoretical criteria and distinctions Max Eastman uses to define, classify, and evaluate humor and laughter (psychological, social, and literary dimensions). Useful for analyzing or teaching about humor broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social bonding / Laughter of Pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is, after speech, the chief thing that holds society together; it is an expression of hospitality and delight — to laugh is to say 'Yes', 'Good!', 'I agree to your emotion!' and functions as a universal welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor partly by its social function: does it invite, welcome, or affirm others? Eastman emphasizes that laughter is a manifestation of social pleasure and acceptance (not rejection), and that the smile and laugh are continuous acts integrated with speech and vision. Anti-pattern: treating laughter merely as an individual overflow or 'side-show' divorced from social utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between true laughter and scorn/derision
rubrics_metrics.description: True laughter (smile/laughter of pleasure) is fundamentally different from scornful expressions (sneer, sarcasm, derision). The temper and neural machinery differ; laughter is an act of acceptance, scorn an act of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or judging humor, separate 'benign' laughter from hostile or sardonic forms. Eastman lists words (gibe, leer, jeer, scoff, flout, hoot, gird, taunt, niggle) and argues these belong to a different family. Anti-pattern: conflating all comic expressions under a single category of 'laughter' without noting hostility or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play as the root of humorous response (Laughter of Playful Pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor originates in the play-attitude: play is an instinctive, spontaneous mode where pleasures are easily obtained and failures become sources of amusement; in play, disappointments often provoke laughter rather than distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a humorous situation invokes a play-like frame (mimicry, non-seriousness, safe failure). Eastman argues that much humor is play's extension into sober life; humor often signals a playful handling of instincts and satisfactions. Examples: rough play, pretend fights, playful disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling as physiological/elementary humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling is the most crude and elementary form of play and provides the authentic primitive picture of humor: sensitive bodily points that would be defended in real combat, when touched in play, produce laughter (a mix of dread and amusement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tickling as a model for why certain stimuli that would be painful in seriousness are amusing in play. Note limitations: one cannot tickle oneself; tickling requires social, play context. This criterion grounds some humor in bodily, evolutionary mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny as mid-position between play and perplexity (element of surprise/disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'funny' occupies a position between play and perplexity: situations that are lightly troubling or that thwart expectations in a non-dangerous way are called funny. Humor often depends on an unexpected or disappointed expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes and humorous effects for their dependence on surprise, mismatch, or thwarted expectation. Eastman points to historical/linguistic development (fonn → fun → funny) to show this conceptual mid-position. Anti-pattern: claiming surprise alone suffices without play-frame/benignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as an adaptive defense / 'making the best of a bad thing'
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of humor functions as an inward shock-absorber or instinct for making the best of disappointment or failure; it enables persistence, experimentation, and protects mental digestion in daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging humor, consider its adaptive, coping function: does it help individuals tolerate failure, persist in efforts, or soften blows? Eastman gives the tack/thumb example and describes humor as 'the most philosophic of all the emotions' for its capacity to relativize good and bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary humor requires an element of loss/failure that is recognized without excessive sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor typically contains something that, if felt too sensitively, would produce tears; the humorous person greets a 'genuine and definite void' where a pleasure was expected with a welcoming twinkle rather than distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the audience's or character's stance is one of tolerant recognition of loss rather than acute suffering; excessive sensitivity undermines humor. This criterion distinguishes hardy, ironic amusement from bitterness or despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure — 'a joke with a point' (point/pivot of a joke)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke typically has a 'point' — an economy of structure that leads to a pivot or unexpected resolution; the point is the essential pivot of comic effect (the discovery or twist that creates the laugh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes for clarity, economy, and presence of a discernible point. Consider timing and variegation: the 'point' should be neither gratuitous nor obscure. Eastman treats 'Jokes with a Point' as a distinct category, implying criteria such as concision, surprise at the pivot, and conceptual sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derision/hostility-based humor (Derision Theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: One family of humor arises from derision or the expression of hostility — laughter directed against others (deriding, sneering, sarcasm). Historically treated as a major explanation for laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing humor, identify whether the laughter is born of contempt or a sense of superiority. Eastman cautions to separate this from benign laughter; this criterion is useful for distinguishing satirical/mocking humor from friendly humor. Ethical evaluation: presence of malice lowers social value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment / thwarted-expectation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises when expectation is thwarted — the 'disappointment' or sudden reversal of expectation produces comic feeling. This is a historical theory Eastman discusses (Disappointment Theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this as an explanatory criterion for many jokes and comic situations: identify the expectation and the nature of its thwarting. Eastman compares and contrasts this with other theories; don't treat it as exclusive — it often combines with play-frame and benignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/physiological accounts of laughter (Mechanical Theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theories explain laughter as mechanical reflexes or physiological discharges (e.g., rhythmic motions, overflow), attempting quantitative mechanics of pleasure-pain oscillation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate biologically-rooted explanations of comic response; Eastman regards some mechanical accounts as aspirational but insufficient alone, because they ignore qualitative aspects of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as liberty / 'laughter as freedom from ends'
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can be understood as a state of mental liberation from the discipline of ends and purposes — a temporary freedom that permits recognition of maladjustment without anxiety (Liberty Theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the comic moment allows ethical or perceptual liberation (recognition of incongruity without moral upset). Eastman presents this as one theoretical dimension among others; useful for analyzing the emancipatory aspect of some comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freudian/unconscious theory of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Freud, jokes and humor release repressed thoughts or unconscious material; laughter is connected to the economy of psychic energy and sublimation of forbidden impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply psychoanalytic criteria when humor seems to covertly express repressed content (sexuality, hostility). Eastman treats Freud's contribution as a major theory to be weighed with others; it's more explanatory of certain types of jokes than a universal rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-mixture theories (mixture of impulses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theories explain laughter as arising from the mixture or conflict of incompatible impulses (e.g., fear + pleasure), producing a comic affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when humor involves simultaneous opposing feelings (e.g., amusement during mild shock). Eastman references conflict-mixture accounts as part of the historical taxonomy; useful to explain ambivalent comic responses like giggling at near-misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as instinct / primary endowment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an argument that the sense of humor is an instinctive endowment — early, spontaneous, specific in its nervous accompaniments (e.g., babies' giggle at forty days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing humor's origins and universality, consider instinctive features: spontaneity, early appearance in children, social character. Eastman uses this to ground many of his claims about play and tickling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and sexuality (sexual sources of comic material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual impulses and situations often provide material and impetus for certain humorous responses; sexuality can flavor the content and dynamics of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether sexual themes are being handled playfully vs. derisively; Eastman treats sexuality as one axis in which humor shows particular characteristics. Consider cultural norms and the play-frame when evaluating such humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor and truth (humor's relation to recognition and insight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often involves recognition of truth — a candid, sometimes skeptical recognition of human foibles — and can reveal truths about life in a way that is insightfully disillusioned rather than destructively cynical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor for its capacity to illuminate truth or produce 'clear-eyed sceptical' perspective (Montaigne as exemplar). Eastman suggests that good humor may provide philosophical insight and ethical moderation rather than mere amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor of quantity (exaggeration, excess, repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative manipulations — exaggeration, overstatement, repetition — produce comic effects (the humor of quantity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedic techniques for whether they use scale or repetition to create incongruity or absurdity. Eastman identifies 'Humor of Quantity' as a formal category useful for literary and practical humor analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical humor (functional/pragmatic uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor as a practical tool: social lubrication, easing tension, enabling perseverance, facilitating experiments, and making life bearable in humdrum pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humor in everyday contexts, prioritize its pragmatic function: does it smooth relations, help coping, or enable social action? Eastman treats practical humor as a distinct domain from poetic or derisive humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic / literary humor (style, devices, and artistic criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic humor employs literary devices (tone, imagery, language, timing) and is judged by artistic criteria (wit, richness, invention) rather than mere sociability or hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary humor by stylistic aptness, imaginative power, and appropriateness to tone (Rabelais and Shakespeare discussed). Eastman separates 'Poetic Humor' as an art-form with distinct standards (e.g., sustained invention, aesthetic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and Bad Jokes (criteria of ethical/aesthetic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good jokes are apt, kind (non-malicious), well-timed, economical, and show perception of the 'point'; bad jokes are cruel, irrelevant, overused, or based on mean hostility or gratuitous hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these evaluative criteria to judge jokes: consider kindness vs cruelty, novelty vs stale repetition, timing, and whether the joke depends on scorn. Eastman devotes a chapter to distinguishing good from bad jokes and emphasizes moral/sociable value as a metric.
